headline: High-risk default interaction: Copilot can feed unverified code into Kestra workflows, creating dangerous action and compliance pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open buffers, while Kestra consumes workflow definitions, YAML, inputs, and variables. If Copilot-generated content is copied into Kestra configs, attacker-controlled text in code or docs can steer workflow logic. The bridge is not automatic, so this is not high, but the shared file-based workflow makes injection plausible.
conditions: IF Copilot output is pasted into Kestra YAML or workflow definitions
IF Kestra parses Copilot-authored text as executable workflow content
mitigations: Review Copilot-suggested YAML before saving
Keep workflow definitions in a separate branch for manual review
Add a lint step for Kestra configs
Restrict Copilot use on files that define automation
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for generated snippets

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers, and Kestra handles logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, database data, and cloud storage data. If the same workspace or copied files are used across both, sensitive material can flow from code-adjacent buffers into Kestra outputs or logs. The profiles do not prove a shared OS workspace, so medium is the safest choice.
conditions: IF sensitive data is present in editor buffers or repo context
IF those contents are transferred into Kestra inputs, variables, or logs
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in repo files
Mask sensitive fields before Kestra ingestion
Review logs for copied code or secrets
Use separate workspaces for code and orchestration
requires-engineering: enforce secret redaction in workflow inputs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state, while Kestra can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, and write files. If both operate on the same repo or storage path, they can race on mutable artifacts and commits without any locking mechanism shown. That overlap makes destructive or inconsistent state likely in default collaborative use.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or directory
IF Kestra tasks modify files while Copilot Workspace applies edits
mitigations: Use separate branches per agent
Pause Kestra writes during Copilot editing
Add file-level locks around shared paths
Require human approval before git commits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces code and edits for human review, while Kestra can execute workflows, send notifications, and interact with cloud services. If Copilot output is promoted into Kestra definitions without verification, Kestra may carry out incorrect or harmful actions at scale. The downstream action authority makes the cascade materially worse than a simple suggestion error.
conditions: IF Copilot-generated workflow text is used as a Kestra task definition
IF Kestra executes or notifies based on that unverified definition
mitigations: Require code review before workflow import
Run a dry-run of Kestra workflows
Compare generated YAML against a template
Limit Kestra permissions for imported jobs
requires-engineering: add schema validation before execution

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is a closed-source vendor service with GitHub repo context and open buffers, while Kestra can process logs, database data, cloud storage data, and notifications across many external systems. If regulated data is placed into Copilot-visible code or then routed through Kestra, residency and retention obligations can diverge. The profiles do not show a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in repo files or editor buffers
IF Kestra routes that data to external services or logs
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of code repositories
Classify data before Kestra workflows run
Review vendor retention settings
Disable unnecessary notification targets
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
